Poverty and Test Performance in NYS Schools

MLDS Boot Camp — Final R Exercise (Solution Key)

Background

The NYC Department of Education asked: what can data tell us about the relationship between poverty and test performance in New York public schools? This report looks at that question using school-level test score data from NYSED and county-level poverty data from the ACS, 2008-2017.

A couple of data quality notes worth surfacing to the department before the results: about 6% of school-year math/ELA scores are missing (coded -99 in the raw file), and roughly 40 rows had free/reduced-lunch percentages above 100%, which we’ve treated as data entry errors and excluded rather than tried to correct.

Visualization 1: FRL Access vs. Test Performance (School Level)

Takeaway: at the individual school level, higher free/reduced-lunch enrollment is associated with lower average math scores — a clear downward trend, though with a lot of school-to-school variation.

Note: Math/ELA Scores Aren’t on a Consistent Scale Across Years

The raw test score range shifts sharply starting in 2013 — this is a change in the test/scoring scheme itself, not a change in student performance, so raw scores from 2008-2012 and 2013-2017 aren’t directly comparable.

Year Min Math Max Math Min ELA Max ELA
2008 536 732 549 715
2009 565 738 564 718
2010 553 738 589 721
2011 570 736 547 696
2012 600 739 600 720
2013 224 366 220 355
2014 230 367 191 356
2015 213 371 195 356
2016 221 375 218 355
2017 222 373 221 363

Takeaway: because of this scale break, Visualizations 1 and 2 (which use raw math/ELA scores) mix scores from both scoring regimes and shouldn’t be read as tracking a single continuous scale. Visualization 3 sidesteps this by using standardized (z-score) values computed within each year, which puts every year on the same scale.

Visualization 2: Test Performance by Poverty Group

Takeaway: average test scores step down consistently from low- to medium- to high-poverty counties, in both subjects.

Visualization 3: Has This Changed Over Time?

Takeaway: the gap between low- and high-poverty counties has held fairly steady across 2008-2017 — there’s no strong evidence the gap is closing on its own.

Summary for the Department

  • Difference between poverty groups: low-poverty counties outperform high-poverty counties in both math and ELA, and the gap is visible from the county level all the way down to individual schools’ lunch program access.
  • Change over time: the gap has persisted rather than narrowed across the ten years of data available here.
  • Moderated by lunch access: yes — FRL access and county poverty tell a consistent story, which strengthens the case that this is a real relationship rather than a quirk of one measure.
  • Caveat: this is a correlational, exploratory analysis done in a short exercise. It doesn’t control for other likely factors (school size, urbanicity, funding levels) and shouldn’t be read as causal.
